newsitem.title: FINLAND: Finland sees debt/GDP ratio below 60% EMU limit in 1996.
newsitem.headline: Finland sees debt/GDP ratio below 60% EMU limit in 1996.

text.p: Finland's gross public debt is likely to fall below the 60 percent of GDP limit for EMU participation already this year and to fall further in 1997, a senior finance ministy official said on Tuesday.

Speaking on condition of anonymity, he told Reuters exact figures were not yet available because calculations were still being made at the ministry's economics department. Official figures would be published in a new forecast due this week.
While delivering a speech, Finance Minister Sauli Niinisto on Tuesday displayed a graph which put Finland's 1997 EMU debt just inside the 60 percent limit.

The information was dated November and attributed to the finance ministry. The ministry's most recent official forecast dated September 3 put Finnish gross public debt to GDP at 61.8 percent in 1996 and at 61.0 percent next year.
"We might well be in a better position than the 61 (percent)," Niinisto told reporters after the speech, but he declined to give any exact figure.

The finance ministry official said it was "highly likely" that the 1997 EMU debt to GDP ratio would be below 60 percent. Asked whether already this year's figure would fall below the EMU entry criterion, he said: "It is possible."
The main factor behind the fall in Finland's EMU debt relative to GDP is that Finnish pension funds have bought more government bonds than expected.
Last week, another senior finance ministry official said the EMU debt to GDP trend had been "more favourable than expected" thanks to bond purchases by the pension funds.

"It is even possible that (domestic pension funds) would gobble up the whole amount of our (the state's) new 1997 net borrowing," he said. Work pension funds' holdings of state paper are deducted from the total outstanding debt when calculating the EMU debt to GDP ratio.

This year's second and third supplementary budgets also reduced the government deficit and the slightly stronger than calculated external value of the markka had marginally reduced Finland's foreign currency debt, the official added.
